title: Exact Local Optimality Does Not Compose: The Complexity of Chronological Realization

paper.title: Exact Local Optimality Does Not Compose: The Complexity of Chronological Realization
paper.abstract:
Abstract The chronological shared realization complexity (CRC) is the smallest
normalized stochastic state dimension C seq C_{\rm seq} needed to reproduce a
collection of future-response menus using one shared family of controlled
transition dynamics. We focus on the rank-tight regime in which both the local
realization dimension and the independent-query static carrier width equal K K , thereby isolating the additional dimensional and computational
constraints imposed by chronological consistency. This framework also serves as the classical baseline for state-dimension
bounds in sequential quantum processes, where stochastic dynamics generalize
to completely positive maps. We establish three results in this regime. First, an explicit payload–delay
family exhibits an unbounded multiplicative state blow-up: C loc = C stat = k C_{\rm loc}=C_{\rm stat}=k while C seq = k ⁡ ( L + 1 ) C_{\rm seq}=k(L+1) , isolating the intrinsic state cost of shared temporal
pullbacks. Second, for explicitly listed rational finite menus over a fixed
five-letter alphabet with a single Boolean terminal effect, exact shared realizability is ∃ ℝ \exists\mathbb{R} -complete, and the zero-versus-inverse-polynomial defect promise problem is 𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗆𝗂𝗌𝖾𝖭𝖯 \mathsf{PromiseNP} -complete, with local and static optima fixed at K K .
Third, a total five-letter chronology compiler translates bounded-rational
Intermediate Simplex instances into a polynomially specified regular geometric
family over the same fixed alphabet, preserving exact local and static width K K . The compiled family yields strong 𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗆𝗂𝗌𝖾𝖭𝖯 \mathsf{PromiseNP} -hardness for
shared realization on strongly bounded-rational inputs, together with an ∃ ℝ \exists\mathbb{R} upper bound certified by an exact polynomial-size finite
core. Together, these results show that exact local and static optimality need not
compose under chronological sharing, even in the rank-tight regime.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction and Main Results
sections.text: Each local prediction table in a family may admit a small normalized stochastic realization, even when no single small state space can support the entire family under shared dynamics. The chronological shared realization complexity (CRC) is this shared dimension C seq C_{\rm seq} . In the normalized classical model, roots are represented by row probability vectors, control actions act on the right as row-stochastic matrices, and responses are evaluated by a single terminal effect written as a column vector. A local model may be chosen independently for each prediction menu. The static relaxation shares a normalized carrier but permits an independent effect per query. CRC requires every query effect to be a pullback M u ​ e M_{u}e generated by the same terminal effect and primitive dynamics. Let K K denote the prescribed bound on the number of latent states; this threshold may vary with the input instance. To isolate the requirement of chronological compatibility, we focus on the rank-tight regime C loc = C stat = K , C_{\rm loc}=C_{\rm stat}=K, where C loc C_{\rm loc} is the largest of the independently minimized local state counts, and C stat C_{\rm stat} is the minimum state count of a shared normalized carrier with independent effects for the tagged queries. In particular, C stat C_{\rm stat} is not the ordinary linear rank of the unaugmented response matrix. Both local realization and static factorization therefore attain the prescribed state budget. The remaining question is whether a chronological shared realization can also attain it, that is, whether C seq = K C_{\rm seq}=K . The results below show that shared chronology can force unbounded multiplicative state overhead and make realizability at this threshold computationally hard to decide. This question is motivated by predictive-state representations (PSRs) and partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs): selected predictive tests may have a low-rank response matrix, while their update rules must remain consistent with future continuations [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Related questions also arise in low-rank partially observed learning [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] and within the broader complexity landscape of partially observed control [ 7 ] . In quantum dynamics, an analogous realization challenge governs sequential state compression and non-Markovian tomographic consistency, where classical stochastic matrices and state distributions generalize to trace-preserving completely positive (CPTP) channels and density operators. Our theorems concern controlled stochastic realization in the normalized model. Rather than analyzing particular learning heuristics or architectural variants, our results isolate the intrinsic structural and computational cost of requiring one chronological shared realization across menus.

sections.heading: From response fitting to chronological closure.
sections.text: The distinction between static fitting and chronological closure is visible even before introducing computationally hard families. Given a root–query response table 𝐑 \mathbf{R} , an independent-effect static realization seeks a factorization 𝐑 = X ​ E \mathbf{R}=XE , where the rows of X X are probability distributions and each query indexes an independently chosen column of E E , subject to the coordinate bounds in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . Once the root carrier X X is fixed, the query columns can be optimized independently. A chronological realization instead replaces these free columns with elements of a shared pullback orbit e , M a ​ e , M b ​ M a ​ e , … . e,\quad M_{a}e,\quad M_{b}M_{a}e,\quad\ldots. Because the same primitive transition matrix may appear in multiple words, modifying a single operator couples an entire family of pulled-back columns. This temporal coupling is not recorded by ordinary matrix rank and remains uncaptured by normalized static carrier width. CRC therefore measures the minimum carrier dimension on which all of these interlocking algebraic identities hold simultaneously. The rank-tight promise makes this distinction sharp. In both hard families, the local witnesses and the independent-query static factorization remain available at width K K ; the additional obstruction is the requirement that all query effects belong to one common pullback orbit. The geometric bounds follow from Theorem 4.1 and Lemma B.1 , while the finite-menu bounds use the identity-calibrated interface of Lemma C.3 .

sections.heading: Scope of the main results.
sections.text: Our results address two structural regimes through three complementary proof mechanisms: • Explicit finite menus (complete classification). For explicitly listed rational instances, exact shared realizability is ∃ ℝ \exists\mathbb{R} -complete via continuous algebraic rigidity, whereas distinguishing zero defect from inverse-polynomial defect is 𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗆𝗂𝗌𝖾𝖭𝖯 \mathsf{PromiseNP} -complete via discrete Boolean isolation and total-variation contraction. • Succinct regular families (separation of bounds). For infinite legal-control languages generated by a total parser, bounded-rational Intermediate Simplex instances yield strong 𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗆𝗂𝗌𝖾𝖭𝖯 \mathsf{PromiseNP} -hardness under strongly bounded-rational, promise-preserving reductions. Exact realizability separately admits an ∃ ℝ \exists\mathbb{R} upper bound by reducing the infinite specification to an exact polynomial-size finite core. These constructions isolate three distinct mathematical mechanisms: continuous algebraic rigidity governs exact real feasibility; Markovian contraction supports the discrete Boolean gap reduction; and interior geometric anchoring, together with finite-core closure, transfers the source geometry to the regular-language setting.

sections.heading: Theoretical context and positioning.
sections.text: Static nonnegative factorization and extension complexity supply the geometric language for carrier width [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] , whereas positive realization and probabilistic automata provide a complementary dynamical viewpoint on shared transitions [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] . CRC places these perspectives within a common normalized realization framework, using a fixed finite alphabet and a single shared terminal effect. The geometric connection is formalized by Theorem 2.4 ; the three regimes are summarized in the table below.

sections.heading: A four-stage proof architecture.
sections.text: The geometric hardness reduction in Theorem 4.1 proceeds through four tightly coupled stages: (1) Geometric embedding and interior anchoring: Embed the bounded-rational Intermediate Simplex source into a normalized carrier and construct an affine anchor basis with inverse-polynomial conditioning. (2) Syntactic compilation: Compile the anchored geometry through a total five-letter parser whose Boolean endpoint signatures force q q pairwise disjoint sectors. Together with the product witness and the endpoint lower bound, this fixes the rank-tight budget at K = k ​ q K=kq . (3) Chronological saturation and simplex recovery: At the saturated budget, recover a single k k -vertex payload simplex and force every recovered primitive transition to preserve that same simplex. (4) Quantitative defect transfer on the finite core: Use the exact finite-core correspondence, together with Hoffman repair bounds and fixed-dimensional orientation estimates, to transfer pointwise response error back to the inverse-polynomial source covering gap. sections.heading: Organization.
sections.text: Section 2 develops the CRC model, the payload–delay separation, and the rank-tight closure principle. Section 3 presents the finite-menu classification theorem and its exact and robust reduction routes. Section 4 introduces the generic chronology compiler and proves the companion geometric hardness result. Section 5 establishes finite-core closure and the corresponding algebraic upper bound, while Section 6 discusses implications and open problems. The main text states the results and proof architecture; the full proofs and constructions are collected in Appendices A – D .

sections.heading: 3 Finite-Menu Classification
sections.text: In this section, the input explicitly lists rational targets for finitely many root–word pairs. Let N N denote the binary encoding length of the finite-menu data and the dimension bound K K . The bound K K is given in unary or is polynomially bounded in N N , and ℓ \ell denotes the maximum listed word length. For the robust problem, a rational tolerance 0 < ϵ < 1 0<\epsilon<1 is supplied as an additional input with encoding length polynomially bounded in N N ; in particular, log ⁡ ( 1 / ϵ ) \log(1/\epsilon) is polynomially bounded in N N . Here J K ​ ( I ) J_{K}(I) denotes the minimax pointwise defect introduced in Definition 2.1 . Response constraints are imposed only on the explicitly listed root–word pairs; there are no additional constraints on unlisted words or infinite control languages. We use promise-preserving polynomial-time many-one reductions: YES instances map to the zero-defect side, J K ​ ( I ) = 0 J_{K}(I)=0 , while NO instances map to the side separated by the prescribed threshold, J K ​ ( I ) ≥ ϵ J_{K}(I)\geq\epsilon . The hardness reductions produce strongly bounded-rational instances: every reduction-generated numerator and denominator has O ⁡ ( log ⁡ N ) O(\log N) bits and hence polynomially bounded magnitude. The robust membership argument allows the general tolerance encoding described above, while the hardness reduction already produces an inverse-polynomial threshold. After compilation through the total five-letter parser of Appendix C , a complete legal-control menu consists of the phase-signature block, the payload identity calibration, and the corresponding post-control phase and payload probes. sections.heading: 6 Discussion and Open Problems
sections.text: Predictive state representations describe controlled systems through action-conditioned predictions rather than an explicit latent-state trajectory [ 1 ] . CRC isolates the corresponding tension in sequential compression: a POMDP or predictive state representation (PSR) may admit low-rank local predictive tests and a low-dimensional normalized static carrier, while a single shared normalized update system may require a substantially larger state dimension. Our payload–delay theorem exhibits this intrinsic state cost, and the two hardness families show that recognizing chronological closure can be computationally intractable in both exact and robust regimes. These results quantify the computational gap between local predictive adequacy and global dynamic realizability (Theorems 2.2 , 3.1 , and 4.1 ). Related issues arise in positive realization, where existence and minimality of positive state-space representations are studied geometrically [ 14 ] . Static factorization compresses a collection of input–output response columns, whereas chronological realization requires every query response to lie in one common pullback orbit generated by shared transition operators. The normalized carrier width C stat C_{\rm stat} measures the former and should not be identified with ordinary matrix rank; CRC measures the latter. This suggests developing approximation frameworks that penalize closure defect explicitly, alongside response error. In finite-sample regimes, empirical sampling perturbs both response tables and estimated update identities. Spectral learning results illustrate how conditioning quantities such as singular-value separation control the recovery of latent dynamical structure [ 3 ] ; determining whether these empirical estimates are compatible with a nearby closed stochastic model constitutes a structured model-selection problem. A natural statistical theory would relate anchor conditioning, the mixing properties of the recovered dynamics, and the metric distance from local predictors to a common invariant carrier, providing a bridge from our worst-case metric transfer bounds to finite-sample learning guarantees. Several structural and parameterized questions remain open: • Fixed-parameter tractability. Proposition B.6 shows that the present hardness construction cannot keep all of its relevant width parameters fixed. It remains open whether tractability holds for sparse, reversible, rapidly mixing, or bounded-treewidth transition structures, or whether hardness persists under alternative parameterizations. • Beyond the rank-tight regime. Finite-core closure here relies on the saturated budget K = k ​ q K=kq , where the calibrated endpoint cells account for the entire carrier. It remains open which observability or minimality conditions restore finite-core certificates when unused latent states are available. • Continuous versus discrete certificates. The finite-menu ∃ ℝ \exists\mathbb{R} reduction permits continuously varying exact witnesses, whereas the robust 𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗆𝗂𝗌𝖾𝖭𝖯 \mathsf{PromiseNP} reduction forces parameters near a Boolean set, yielding polynomial-size certificates for the promised defect gap. It remains an intriguing question which dynamical families guarantee polynomially encodable and exactly verifiable discrete, rational, or algebraic certificates for exact realizability itself. • Improved robust transfer. It is open whether stronger conditioning assumptions or alternative geometric sources yield sharper robustness exponents while retaining the chronological hardness gap. • Quantum dynamical analogues. A natural noncommutative extension would replace probability vectors by density operators, stochastic updates by CPTP maps, and terminal effects by POVM effects. Outcome-labeled controls would then correspond to quantum instruments. Determining whether quantum shared realization exhibits analogous dimensional gaps or distinct algebraic obstructions presents a compelling frontier.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2609.19707v1 [quant-ph] 17 Sep 2026 Exact Local Optimality Does Not Compose: The Complexity of Chronological Realization Yixin Zhao zhaoyixin22@mails.ucas.ac.cn Affiliation: Beijing Key Laboratory of Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing, Beijing Academy of Quantum Information Sciences, Beijing 100193, China Affiliation: Beijing National Laboratory for Condensed Matter Physics, Institute of Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China Affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China Abstract The chronological shared realization complexity (CRC) is the smallest normalized stochastic state dimension C seq C_{\rm seq} needed to reproduce a collection of future-response menus using one shared family of controlled transition dynamics. We focus on the rank-tight regime in which both the local realization dimension and the independent-query static carrier width equal K K , thereby isolating the additional dimensional and computational constraints imposed by chronological consistency. This framework also serves as the classical baseline for state-dimension bounds in sequential quantum processes, where stochastic dynamics generalize to completely positive maps. We establish three results in this regime. First, an explicit payload–delay family exhibits an unbounded multiplicative state blow-up: C loc = C stat = k C_{\rm loc}=C_{\rm stat}=k while C seq = k ⁡ ( L + 1 ) C_{\rm seq}=k(L+1) , isolating the intrinsic state cost of shared temporal pullbacks. Second, for explicitly listed rational finite menus over a fixed five-letter alphabet with a single Boolean terminal effect, exact shared realizability is ∃ ℝ \exists\mathbb{R} -complete, and the zero-versus-inverse-polynomial defect promise problem is 𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗆𝗂𝗌𝖾𝖭𝖯 \mathsf{PromiseNP} -complete, with local and static optima fixed at K K . Third, a total five-letter chronology compiler translates bounded-rational Intermediate Simplex instances into a polynomially specified regular geometric family over the same fixed alphabet, preserving exact local and static width K K . The compiled family yields strong 𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗆𝗂𝗌𝖾𝖭𝖯 \mathsf{PromiseNP} -hardness for shared realization on strongly bounded-rational inputs, together with an ∃ ℝ \exists\mathbb{R} upper bound certified by an exact polynomial-size finite core. Together, these results show that exact local and static optimality need not compose under chronological sharing, even in the rank-tight regime. 1 Introduction and Main Results Each local prediction table in a family may admit a small normalized stochastic realization, even when no single small state space can support the entire family under shared dynamics. The chronological shared realization complexity (CRC) is this shared dimension C seq C_{\rm seq} . In the normalized classical model, roots are represented by row probability vectors, control actions act on the right as row-stochastic matrices, and responses are evaluated by a single terminal effect written as a column vector. A local model may be chosen independently for each prediction menu. The static relaxation shares a normalized carrier but permits an independent effect per query. CRC requires every query effect to be a pullback M u ​ e M_{u}e generated by the same terminal effect and primitive dynamics. Let K K denote the prescribed bound on the number of latent states; this threshold may vary with the input instance. To isolate the requirement of chronological compatibility, we focus on the rank-tight regime C loc = C stat = K , C_{\rm loc}=C_{\rm stat}=K, where C loc C_{\rm loc} is the largest of the independently minimized local state counts, and C stat C_{\rm stat} is the minimum state count of a shared normalized carrier with independent effects for the tagged queries. In particular, C stat C_{\rm stat} is not the ordinary linear rank of the unaugmented response matrix. Both local realization and static factorization therefore attain the prescribed state budget. The remaining question is whether a chronological shared realization can also attain it, that is, whether C seq = K C_{\rm seq}=K . The results below show that shared chronology can force unbounded multiplicative state overhead and make realizability at this threshold computationally hard to decide. This question is motivated by predictive-state representations (PSRs) and partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs): selected predictive tests may have a low-rank response matrix, while their update rules must remain consistent with future continuations [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Related questions also arise in low-rank partially observed learning [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] and within the broader complexity landscape of partially observed control [ 7 ] . In quantum dynamics, an analogous realization challenge governs sequential state compression and non-Markovian tomographic consistency, where classical stochastic matrices and state distributions generalize to trace-preserving completely positive (CPTP) channels and density operators. Our theorems concern controlled stochastic realization in the normalized model. Rather than analyzing particular learning heuristics or architectural variants, our results isolate the intrinsic structural and computational cost of requiring one chronological shared realization across menus. From response fitting to chronological closure. The distinction between static fitting and chronological closure is visible even before introducing computationally hard families. Given a root–query response table 𝐑 \mathbf{R} , an independent-effect static realization seeks a factorization 𝐑 = X ​ E \mathbf{R}=XE , where the rows of X X are probability distributions and each query indexes an independently chosen column of E E , subject to the coordinate bounds in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . Once the root carrier X X is fixed, the query columns can be optimized independently. A chronological realization instead replaces these free columns with elements of a shared pullback orbit e , M a ​ e , M b ​ M a ​ e , … . e,\quad M_{a}e,\quad M_{b}M_{a}e,\quad\ldots. Because the same primitive transition matrix may appear in multiple words, modifying a single operator couples an entire family of pulled-back columns. This temporal coupling is not recorded by ordinary matrix rank and remains uncaptured by normalized static carrier width. CRC therefore measures the minimum carrier dimension on which all of these interlocking algebraic identities hold simultaneously. The rank-tight promise makes this distinction sharp. In both hard families, the local witnesses and the independent-query static factorization remain available at width K K ; the additional obstruction is the requirement that all query effects belong to one common pullback orbit. The geometric bounds follow from Theorem 4.1 and Lemma B.1 , while the finite-menu bounds use the identity-calibrated interface of Lemma C.3 . Scope of the main results. Our results address two structural regimes through three complementary proof mechanisms: • Explicit finite menus (complete classification). For explicitly listed rational instances, exact shared realizability is ∃ ℝ \exists\mathbb{R} -complete via continuous algebraic rigidity, whereas distinguishing zero defect from inverse-polynomial defect is 𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗆𝗂𝗌𝖾𝖭𝖯 \mathsf{PromiseNP} -complete via discrete Boolean isolation and total-variation contraction. • Succinct regular families (separation of bounds). For infinite legal-control languages generated by a total parser, bounded-rational Intermediate Simplex instances yield strong 𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗆𝗂𝗌𝖾𝖭𝖯 \mathsf{PromiseNP} -hardness under strongly bounded-rational, promise-preserving reductions. Exact realizability separately admits an ∃ ℝ \exists\mathbb{R} upper bound by reducing the infinite specification to an exact polynomial-size finite core. These constructions isolate three distinct mathematical mechanisms: continuous algebraic rigidity governs exact real feasibility; Markovian contraction supports the discrete Boolean gap reduction; and interior geometric anchoring, together with finite-core closure, transfers the source geometry to the regular-language setting. Theoretical context and positioning. Static nonnegative factorization and extension complexity supply the geometric language for carrier width [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] , whereas positive realization and probabilistic automata provide a complementary dynamical viewpoint on shared transitions [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] . CRC places these perspectives within a common normalized realization framework, using a fixed finite alphabet and a single shared terminal effect. The geometric connection is formalized by Theorem 2.4 ; the three regimes are summarized in the table below. A four-stage proof architecture. The geometric hardness reduction in Theorem 4.1 proceeds through four tightly coupled stages: (1) Geometric embedding and interior anchoring: Embed the bounded-rational Intermediate Simplex source into a normalized carrier and construct an affine anchor basis with inverse-polynomial conditioning. (2) Syntactic compilation: Compile the anchored geometry through a total five-letter parser whose Boolean endpoint signatures force q q pairwise disjoint sectors. Together with the product witness and the endpoint lower bound, this fixes the rank-tight budget at K = k ​ q K=kq . (3) Chronological saturation and simplex recovery: At the saturated budget, recover a single k k -vertex payload simplex and force every recovered primitive transition to preserve that same simplex. (4) Quantitative defect transfer on the finite core: Use the exact finite-core correspondence, together with Hoffman repair bounds and fixed-dimensional orientation estimates, to transfer pointwise response error back to the inverse-polynomial source covering gap.
